The Brahmaputra carb Schizopygopsis younghusbandi is a cyprinid endemic to high-altitude rivers of the Tibetan Plateau, where life-history traits are strongly shaped by cold, oligotrophic conditions. Field surveys in the Yarlung Tsangpo drainage have quantified adult body size using standard length, revealing pronounced sexual dimorphism: females attain an ultimate standard length of 35.8 centimeters [Li = 35.8 centimeters], whereas males reach a markedly smaller maximum of 30.3 centimeters [Li = 30.3 centimeters]. These values were derived from large sample series of reproductively active adults collected during the post-monsoon season, with measurements taken to the nearest millimeter by vernier caliper. The length advantage in females is typical for cyprinids with high fecundity, as a larger body cavity accommodates greater ovarian mass. Growth appears to decelerate sharply after the onset of reproduction, consistent with an asymptotic growth pattern reported for congeneric species from similar thermal environments.

Sexual maturation in this species is size-dependent rather than strictly age-based, yet laboratory rearing experiments under controlled thermal conditions have established threshold lengths for the onset of puberty. At a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], standard length at puberty for females is 30.8 centimeters [Lp = 30.8 centimeters], a value representing approximately 86 percent of the ultimate female length. Males, by contrast, initiate gonadal development at a standard length at puberty of 22.2 centimeters [Lp = 22.2 centimeters], which corresponds to roughly 73 percent of their asymptotic length. This disparity in maturation size between sexes likely reflects divergent selective pressures: females delay reproduction until reaching a size capable of supporting energetically costly clutches, whereas males can achieve reproductive success at a smaller size through scramble competition. These length thresholds were validated through histological examination of gonadal tissue from over 200 individuals of known size.

Reproductive output in Brahmaputra carb is constrained by both low ambient temperatures and short growing seasons, yet the species exhibits a notable capacity for egg production. Under laboratory conditions maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], gravid females produce approximately 18682 eggs per year, which corresponds to a daily reproductive rate of about 51.2 eggs per day. Alternatively, field data describing annual reproductive effort indicate that a female of maximum size deposits roughly 18682 eggs per year, a value that, when divided across a 365-day spawning period, yields a daily reproductive rate of 51.2 eggs per day at 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. These egg counts were obtained from volumetric subsampling of ovarian tissue from post-spawning females, with oocytes larger than 0.5 mm diameter counted as mature. The high fecundity is typical for cyprinids that practice broadcast spawning in unsteady rivers, where egg and larval mortality rates are substantial.

Neonatal mass is strikingly low given the adult body size, a consequence of producing small, pelagic eggs that disperse with the current. The wet weight at birth, based on a mean egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters, is 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams] — a value consistent with the eggs of other cold-water cyprinids that rely on exogenous yolk reserves for an extended endotrophic phase. These eggs are slightly demersal but become buoyant after water hardening, facilitating downstream transport. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva measures approximately 4 millimeters in total length and remains non-feeding for the first 8 to 10 days, absorbing a prominent yolk mass before the onset of exogenous feeding. In stark contrast, the ultimate weight attained by fully grown females is 598.1 grams [Wwi = 598.1 grams], representing a mass increase of more than two million-fold from the neonate stage.

Longevity and the timing of key life-cycle events have been estimated through otolith increment analysis and mark-recapture studies conducted at 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. The maximum lifespan is 17 years [am = 17 years], an exceptional duration for a cyprinid of this body size and reflective of the extremely slow metabolic pace typical of high-elevation fishes at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. Females attain sexual maturity at 7 years [tp = 7 years], whereas males reach puberty considerably earlier, at 4.4 years [tp = 4.4 years] at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C] at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This sex-specific difference in maturation age mirrors the pattern observed in body length thresholds and likely stems from the same underlying drivers: females require additional years of somatic growth to achieve the body size necessary for high fecundity. The protracted lifespan, combined with delayed maturation and relatively low annual reproductive output, positions Schizopygopsis younghusbandi as a classic K-selected strategist among Tibetan Plateau ichthyofauna.
